Family Health

Hair-dye reactions: what to do and what to avoid

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Itching, swelling or burning after hair colouring can come from irritation or an allergy. Stop exposure first, check for urgent symptoms and get advice before trying another dye or a home chemical remedy.

Irritation and allergy are different reactions

Hair dye contains several chemicals that can affect the skin. Irritant contact dermatitis happens when a product directly damages or irritates the skin barrier. Allergic contact dermatitis involves an immune response to an ingredient. Both can cause burning, itching, dryness or a rash, so symptoms alone do not always tell them apart.

A reaction can occur even after years of apparently trouble-free use. Becoming sensitised does not necessarily produce symptoms at the first exposure. Once an allergy has developed, using the same ingredient again can trigger another reaction, sometimes more quickly or more severely. A familiar brand is therefore not a guarantee of future tolerance.

Why PPD is often involved

Paraphenylenediamine, usually shortened to PPD, is used in many permanent and some semi-permanent dyes. In an oxidative dye, colour ingredients and a developer are mixed before application. Intermediate products formed during oxidation can trigger allergy in a sensitised person.

Darker shades often contain more PPD, but colour alone cannot establish what is in a product or whether it is suitable for you. PPD has uses beyond hair colouring, including some dyes and photographic processes. Black temporary “henna” tattoos are a particularly important exposure because added PPD can sensitise the skin before a person ever reacts to hair dye.

Recognise local and spreading symptoms

Symptoms may appear during colouring, several hours later or up to about 72 hours afterward. Look for itching, stinging, tightness, soreness, dryness, blisters or swelling. The scalp, hairline, ears, eyelids, face and neck may be affected, and a more extensive rash can spread beyond the areas directly touched by dye.

Redness can be less obvious on darker skin; changes may look purple, grey or darker brown. Marked eyelid or facial swelling, widespread painful skin changes or symptoms that continue to worsen need prompt medical advice. Swollen hands or other areas can also be part of a broader reaction, rather than a problem confined to the hair.

Know the signs of an emergency

Rarely, hair dye can cause anaphylaxis. Sudden swelling of the tongue, throat, lips or mouth, difficulty breathing or swallowing, a hoarse voice, severe dizziness or collapse needs an ambulance. A rash may occur, but its absence does not make airway or circulation symptoms safe. Nausea or vomiting can accompany a severe reaction.

Use a prescribed adrenaline auto-injector immediately if anaphylaxis is suspected and call emergency services. Lie down; if breathing is difficult, raise the upper body carefully. Do not stand, walk or drive yourself to hospital. Follow the emergency operator’s instructions, including advice about a second injector. Antihistamines are not a substitute for adrenaline and emergency care.

Stop exposure and remove the dye

If a reaction starts, stop applying the product. Wash the hair and scalp thoroughly with water and a mild shampoo to remove remaining dye. Do not keep it on to finish the colour, and do not apply a second colouring product to correct the result.

Keep the packaging or a clear photograph of the full ingredient list, product name and shade. Record when it was applied and when symptoms began. These details can help a pharmacist or clinician choose treatment and later identify the cause. Seek help promptly if the reaction is worsening, affects the eyes, is extensive or interferes with normal activities.

Treatment should match the symptoms and the skin site

For a mild reaction, a pharmacist may suggest an emollient or an appropriate antihistamine for itching. A clinician may prescribe a topical corticosteroid to reduce dermatitis, or sometimes tablets for a more severe reaction. Some antihistamines cause drowsiness, so ask about driving, other medicines and pregnancy or breastfeeding if relevant.

Do not assume an over-the-counter steroid is suitable for every area. Facial skin, eyelids and other sensitive sites need specific advice. Clobetasol scalp products are potent prescription treatments, not routine shampoos to try for an unexplained reaction. Steroid eye drops, ear drops, creams and tablets are not interchangeable; use only the formulation and course prescribed for the problem.

Avoid improvised chemical treatments

Do not put household hydrogen peroxide or a homemade potassium permanganate mixture onto the reaction. Concentration, preparation and the condition of the skin matter, and an attempted chemical treatment can add irritation or cause a burn.

Some specialist descriptions discuss oxidising residual PPD, but that is not a general self-treatment instruction. Potassium permanganate has specific clinical uses with carefully prepared dilutions and storage precautions. If it is prescribed, follow the supplied directions exactly. Never swallow it or leave it where it could be mistaken for an oral medicine.

Read ingredients rather than marketing claims

“Natural”, “herbal” and “ammonia-free” do not mean allergy-free. PPD may be written as paraphenylenediamine, para-phenylenediamine or p-phenylenediamine. Other names include p-diaminobenzene, 1,4-diaminobenzene, 1,4-benzenediamine and 4-aminoaniline; PPD and PPDA are abbreviations used in discussions of the ingredient.

PPD is not the only possible cause. Other colourants, fragrances, preservatives or resorcinol can be relevant, while alkaline ingredients and peroxide can irritate the skin. A “PPD-free” formula may still contain a related dye or another allergen. Take uncertain names to a pharmacist, dermatologist or the manufacturer rather than deciding from one reassuring word on the front of the box.

Understand the limits of testing at home

Before ordinary use, follow the product’s allergy-alert instructions every time, including its waiting interval. A previous negative result does not guarantee that a full application will be tolerated. A strand test mainly checks the effect on hair; it is not the same as a diagnostic skin-allergy assessment.

If you have already reacted to dye or a black henna tattoo, do not deliberately re-expose yourself at home to see whether the allergy has gone away. A dermatologist can arrange patch testing with selected ingredients and an appropriate concentration. Testing itself can provoke a reaction, so the method should reflect the history, especially after a severe episode.

Choose alternatives with an allergy plan

Pure henna, indigo, vegetable rinses and some non-permanent products may be options for some people, but none is universally safe. “Black henna” can contain PPD, and plant ingredients can themselves cause reactions. An independent or additive-free claim does not prove that a product avoids your particular allergen.

Some people allergic to PPD also react to related dyes, including ingredients used in alternatives. Wait until the reaction has settled and seek ingredient-specific advice before colouring again. Avoiding dye altogether is a valid choice. Tell a salon about the reaction before any product is applied, even if you plan to change brands or shades.

Share the allergy history with other clinicians

Tell your doctor, dentist and hairdresser about confirmed or suspected PPD allergy. Related substances can sometimes cross-react; benzocaine and procaine are examples discussed in allergy references. This does not mean every local anaesthetic is unsafe or that you should label yourself allergic to all dental injections.

A clinician can review the actual patch-test result and the medicine being proposed. Keep a written record of the ingredient that caused the reaction and any advice about alternatives. Occupational exposure may also matter for hairdressers or people working with dyes, who may need guidance on gloves and reducing skin contact.

Reducing the chance of another reaction

For someone without a known allergy, follow the label, wear suitable gloves, avoid leaving dye on beyond the recommended time and rinse thoroughly. Do not combine different products, and do not use ordinary hair dye on eyebrows or eyelashes. Store it away from children.

After a suspected allergic reaction, stopping the culprit product and clarifying the ingredient is more useful than repeatedly trying small amounts. Symptoms that do not settle, recur without an obvious exposure or spread despite treatment need review. The aim is a practical avoidance plan, rather than assuming that a lighter shade or a “natural” label solves the problem.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Irritant and allergic dermatitis can look similar; a product label or symptom pattern does not identify the culprit by itself.

A previous uneventful application or negative home test cannot guarantee future tolerance.

How BeMama can help

Save the product label and a brief symptom timeline to make a pharmacy or dermatology discussion more useful.

When to seek help

Sudden mouth or throat swelling, breathing difficulty or collapse needs emergency treatment. Use prescribed adrenaline for suspected anaphylaxis and call an ambulance.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • PPD is a common culprit, but other ingredients can matter.
  • Symptoms can be delayed for up to about three days.
  • Wash off the dye and avoid further exposure.
  • Do not improvise peroxide, permanganate or potent steroid treatment.
  • Choose future products using an ingredient-specific allergy plan.

Frequently asked questions

Can I react after using the same dye for years?

Yes. Sensitisation can develop over time. Previous tolerance does not rule out a new allergy, and further exposure may cause a stronger reaction.

Does a reaction always begin straight away?

No. It may start during application or be delayed for hours to around 72 hours. Record the timing and seek advice if symptoms worsen or spread.

Should I finish the colouring before washing it off?

No. Stop application and remove the product with water and a mild shampoo. Do not add another chemical product to correct the colour or neutralise the reaction.

Can an antihistamine treat anaphylaxis?

No. Airway symptoms, sudden mouth or throat swelling, severe dizziness or collapse require emergency care and prescribed adrenaline if available. Do not wait to see whether an antihistamine works.

Can I put hydrocortisone on swollen eyelids?

Ask a pharmacist or clinician first. The face and eye area need a suitable diagnosis, strength and duration; an ordinary skin product is not automatically appropriate.

Why not use peroxide or potassium permanganate at home?

Incorrect products or dilutions can irritate or burn already affected skin. Specialist chemical treatments should not be turned into improvised home recipes.

Does PPD-free mean safe for a PPD allergy?

Not necessarily. Related dyes and other allergens may still be present. Review the whole formulation with a clinician who knows the allergy result.

Is pure henna always safe?

No product is safe for everyone. Pure henna differs from black henna containing added PPD, but plant ingredients can also cause reactions. Verify the formulation and your individual suitability.

Should I retest a dye after a previous reaction?

Do not deliberately challenge a suspected allergy yourself. Ask about professional patch testing and future avoidance. A negative consumer test is not a guarantee.

Does PPD allergy mean I cannot have dental anaesthesia?

No. Some related substances, including benzocaine or procaine, may be relevant, but not all local anaesthetics are equivalent. Tell the dentist the exact allergy history so a suitable option can be chosen.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
